01.note: Rabbi Akiva is in prison when his student Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai asks him to teach him Torah. Rabbi Akiva refuses because teaching is dangerous. Rabbi Shimon jokes that if he is refused, he will tell his father Yohai, who will hand Rabbi Akiva over to the government. Rabbi Akiva answers that the cow wants to nurse even more than the calf wants to suck; Rabbi Shimon replies that the calf is the one in danger. Rabbi Akiva then gives him advice: if you want to strangle yourself, hang yourself on a tall tree, and teach your son from a corrected text.
01.why: The Gemara has just quoted seven instructions Rabbi Akiva gave his son, Rabbi Yehoshua. It moves on to a second set of his teachings, given to Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai in prison, and the Gemara explains each saying as it goes.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A teacher held in prison, who is asked to keep teaching Torah while he is there.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's student, who pushes him to go on teaching.

people.name: Yohai
people.about: Rabbi Shimon's father, named in Rabbi Shimon's joking threat.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who explains what 'teach him from a corrected text' means. Some say it was Rav Mesharshiya.

terms.term: Hang yourself on a tall tree
terms.meaning: A proverb. As the Gemara explains it, a person who wants people to accept what he says should credit it to a great man.
A copy that has been checked for mistakes. The Gemara explains why it matters: once a mistake gets into a learner's mind, it is hard to get out.

01.flag: The story stops after two of the five instructions it promises; the other three continue in the AFTER segments.

02.note: Demons once roamed every day. Agrat, daughter of Mahalat, met Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa and told him she would have put him in danger if Heaven had not announced: 'Be careful of Hanina and his Torah.' He answered that if he really mattered in Heaven, he decreed that she must never pass through places where people live. She begged him to leave her a little room, so he left her Shabbat nights and Tuesday nights.
02.why: A baraita has just warned against going out alone on Tuesday and Friday nights, because Agrat and her destroying angels go out then. This story explains why those two nights in particular are the dangerous ones.

people.name: Agrat, daughter of Mahalat
people.about: A demon who threatens Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A Sage whose Torah Heaven has told everyone to respect. He limits where the demon may go.

03.note: Agrat, daughter of Mahalat, met Abaye and told him she would have put him in danger if Heaven had not announced: 'Be careful of Nahmani and his Torah.' Abaye answered that if he really mattered in Heaven, he decreed that she must never pass through places where people live. The Gemara then objects that demons are still seen in such places. The Sages answer that those are demons on the paths near town, chasing their own runaway horses.
03.why: This follows the matching story about Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, who banned the demon from inhabited places except on two nights. The Gemara uses Abaye's ban to ask why demons are still seen near towns.

people.name: Agrat, daughter of Mahalat
people.about: A demon who threatens Abaye.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage, called Nahmani in Heaven's announcement, who bans the demon from inhabited places.

04.note: Tuveya committed a sexual sin, and Zigud came alone to testify against him before Rav Pappa. Rav Pappa had Zigud lashed. Zigud protested: 'Tuveya sinned and Zigud is lashed?' Rav Pappa answered yes, because the Torah says one witness may not rise up against a man, so his lone testimony only gave Tuveya a bad name.
04.why: The Gemara has just listed three people God hates, among them a man who sees another commit a sexual sin and testifies against him alone. This case shows a court punishing exactly that kind of lone witness.

people.name: Tuveya
people.about: A man accused of a sexual sin.

people.name: Zigud
people.about: The only witness against Tuveya. He is lashed for testifying alone.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who hears the testimony and orders Zigud lashed.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law a person can be convicted only on the testimony of two witnesses. One witness alone cannot prove a case.
Flogged as a punishment ordered by a court.

05.note: Rav Nahman asked his servant Daru: when a master frees his slave and gives him silver and gold, what should the slave say to him? Daru answered that the slave should thank and praise his master. Rav Nahman told him that he had just spared them from asking the questions that begin 'Why is this night different,' and he went straight on to recite: 'We were slaves.'
05.why: The mishna says the father's answer at the seder begins with disgrace. Shmuel says that disgrace is 'We were slaves.' Rav Nahman opens with exactly those words once Daru's answer has already said what the questions were meant to bring out.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage leading the seder, who questions his servant.

people.name: Daru
people.about: Rav Nahman's servant, whose answer moves the seder forward.

terms.meaning: The questions asked at the Passover seder meal, meant to get the children asking. The father's answer to them tells the story of leaving Egypt.
The opening words of the answer to the seder questions: we were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt, and God brought us out.

06.note: Ravina tells of a visit to Mareimar in Sura. The prayer leader there recited the prayer in the version of the Elders of Pumbedita, and everyone tried to silence him, because they did not know that version. Mareimar told them to leave him alone, since the law follows the Elders of Pumbedita. After that, nobody tried to silence him.
06.why: The Gemara has been arguing over the exact wording of the Festival blessing. After reports that Rava and Rav Pappa accepted the Elders of Pumbedita's version, Ravina's report shows Mareimar ruling outright that the law follows it.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who tells what he saw on a visit to Sura.

people.name: Mareimar
people.about: The Sage in Sura who tells the congregation to let the prayer leader finish.

terms.meaning: The person who leads the congregation in prayer, reciting it aloud on their behalf.
The senior Sages of Pumbedita, a center of Torah learning in Babylonia. They had their own version of the Festival prayer's wording.
Jewish law: the ruling that is actually followed in practice.

07.note: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Papeyyas testified that the offspring of an animal set aside as a peace-offering must itself be sacrificed as a peace-offering. Rabbi Papeyyas gave a case from his own family: they had a cow that was a peace-offering and ate it on Passover, and they ate its calf as a peace-offering on the Festival.
07.why: Rava has just said that a person who lets even one Festival pass without bringing an offering he owes breaks a positive commandment. Rabbi Papeyyas's family seems to have waited past Shavuot, so the Gemara raises his account as an objection to Rava.

people.name: Rabbi Papeyyas
people.about: A Sage who testifies about what his family did with a peace-offering cow and its calf.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who testifies together with Rabbi Papeyyas about the law.

terms.meaning: An animal sacrifice brought to the Temple. Most of its meat was eaten by the owners at a festive meal.
Here the translation takes it to mean Sukkot, the autumn festival. The Gemara later discusses whether it could mean Shavuot.
Gave formal evidence before the Sages about what the law is, based on a tradition or on events the speaker saw.

08.note: Rabbi Akiva picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and set aside two different tithes from it, one following Beit Shammai and one following Beit Hillel, because their rulings put that day in different tithe years. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda disagrees about why he did it: he says Rabbi Akiva was not following Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel but the conflicting practices of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.
08.why: The mishna has just given the first of Shevat as the new year for trees, according to Beit Shammai. Rabbi Akiva's double tithe shows a Sage caught between the two dates. The Gemara then asks whether he was allowed to follow two opposing rulings at once.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who picks an etrog and sets aside two tithes from it because he is unsure of the law.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who gives a different reason for Rabbi Akiva's two tithes.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on how an etrog is tithed is one of the two Rabbi Akiva follows, according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose ruling on how an etrog is tithed is the other one, according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A citron, a citrus fruit used in the rituals of the Sukkot festival.
Portions of produce that had to be set aside by law. Which tithe was due depended on the year of the seven-year cycle the fruit belonged to.
The schools of two early Sages, Shammai and Hillel, who disagreed on many points of law. Here they disagree over whether the new year for trees falls on the first or the fifteenth of Shevat.
A winter month in the Hebrew calendar.

09.note: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, fell ill, and Rav Pappa came to visit him. Seeing that he was dying, Rav Pappa told those present to prepare his shrouds. In the end Rav Huna recovered, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed to see him. When asked what he had seen, Rav Huna said he really had been close to death. But the Holy One told the heavenly court that since Rav Huna did not insist on his rights against others, they should not be strict with him either.
09.why: Rava has just taught, from the verse 'He bears sin and forgives transgression,' that God forgives the sins of a person who lets go of the wrongs others did him. Rav Huna's recovery is told as an example, and he quotes the same verse.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who comes close to death and recovers. He tells what was decided about him in Heaven.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who visits Rav Huna, has his shrouds prepared, and is later embarrassed when he recovers.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who tells the heavenly court to be lenient with Rav Huna.

terms.meaning: A polite word for burial shrouds, the cloth in which the dead are wrapped.

terms.term: Does not stand on his rights
terms.meaning: Lets go of what others owe him and does not insist on getting back at people who wronged him.

10.note: Rava says the sin of Eli's house cannot be atoned for with sacrifices but can be atoned for through Torah study. Abaye says it can be atoned for through Torah study together with acts of kindness. The Gemara then reports that Rabba and Abaye were both descended from the house of Eli. Rabba, who studied Torah, lived forty years; Abaye, who studied Torah and did acts of kindness, lived sixty.
10.why: Rabbi Yonatan has just taught, from God's oath against the house of Eli, that a sentence sealed with an oath cannot be cancelled. Rava and Abaye limit that oath to sacrifices, and the lives of Rabba and Abaye are given as evidence for their view.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who says Torah study can atone for the sin of Eli's house.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli. He studied Torah and did acts of kindness, and lived sixty years.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage descended from the house of Eli. He studied Torah and lived forty years.

terms.meaning: The family of Eli, a priest in the Bible. God swore that their sin would never be atoned for with sacrifice or offering.
Good deeds done for other people, such as helping, visiting or supporting them.

11.note: There was a family in Jerusalem whose members kept dying at eighteen. They came and told Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai. He said they might be descended from the family of Eli, of whom it is written that all the increase of the house would die young men. He told them to go and study Torah and they would live. They studied Torah and lived, and people called the family by Rabban Yohanan's name.
11.why: The Gemara has just said that the curse on the house of Eli cannot be atoned for with sacrifices but can be through Torah study. This baraita shows Torah study lifting that curse.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage the family turns to. He tells them to study Torah.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was left out of the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law, but is quoted in the Gemara.
The descendants of Eli, a priest in the Bible. Scripture says that its members would die young.

12.note: Once the Sages decreed a fast on Hanukkah in the town of Lod. Rabbi Eliezer went down and bathed, and Rabbi Yehoshua went down and had his hair cut, to show they did not accept the fast. They told the others to go out and fast another fast to make up for the fast they had already kept.
12.why: Rav and Rabbi Hanina say the festive days listed in Megillat Ta'anit no longer apply. Rav Kahana raises this incident against them, since Hanukkah is one of those days and the Sages still would not allow a fast on it.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who bathes on the fast day to show he rejects it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who has his hair cut on the fast day to show he rejects it.

terms.meaning: An ancient list of joyful days, commemorating good events, on which fasting and eulogies were forbidden.
Things a person refrains from on a public fast. Doing them showed that the Sages did not treat the day as a fast.

13.note: The wicked kingdom had banned Torah study and circumcision and ordered Jews to break Shabbat. Yehuda ben Shammua and his colleagues went for advice to a matron whom the leading men of Rome visited. She told them to go and cry out at night. They cried out at night: 'O Heavens! Are we not your brothers, children of one father and one mother? Why are we different from every nation, that you issue harsh decrees against us?' The decrees were cancelled, and the day was made a festive day.
13.why: The Gemara is asking whether the festive days of Megillat Ta'anit were later cancelled. Rav Tovi bar Mattana raises this day as an objection: it was added later, so how could the earlier days have been dropped while new ones were being added?

terms.meaning: A noble Roman woman. This one was visited by the most important men of Rome, so she was asked how to get the decree overturned.
An ancient list of joyful days, commemorating good events, on which fasting and eulogies were forbidden.

13.flag: The story begins mid-scene with 'She said to them'; the decree, Yehuda ben Shammua and the visit to the matron are in the preceding BEFORE segment.

14.note: Levi arrived in Babylonia on the day the people there counted as the eleventh of Tishrei. He remarked how tasty the Babylonians' food was on the very day Yom Kippur was being kept in the Land of Israel, where the date was a day behind. The people asked him to testify, so that they could keep Yom Kippur that day. He refused, saying he had not himself heard the court declare the month sanctified.
14.why: The Gemara is discussing how Jews outside the Land of Israel kept festival days when they were unsure how the court there had fixed the month. Levi's visit shows the two communities on different days, and that a witness must have heard the court himself.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who travels from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and notices the calendar difference.

terms.meaning: The autumn month that begins with Rosh HaShana. Yom Kippur falls on its tenth day.
What the Babylonian Sages called the Land of Israel, which lay to their west.
The words the court in the Land of Israel said aloud when it officially declared a new month. That declaration fixed the date of the festivals.

15.note: Rabbi Aivu bar Naggarei and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba came to a place that the messengers announcing the new month reached in Nisan but not in Tishrei. The people there kept only one day of Passover, and the two Sages said nothing. Rabbi Yohanan heard and was angry. He told them: 'Did I not tell you that wherever the Nisan messengers arrive but the Tishrei messengers do not, they must keep two days, a decree for Nisan because of Tishrei?'
15.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Yohanan's rule that such places must keep two days of Passover, so that they would not come to keep Sukkot for only one day. This story shows how seriously he took it.

people.name: Rabbi Aivu bar Naggarei
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yohanan who did not correct the local practice.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yohanan who traveled with Rabbi Aivu and also kept silent.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Their teacher, who was angry that they did not enforce his ruling.

terms.meaning: Riders sent out from the court in the Land of Israel to tell distant communities which day the month had begun, so they would know when to keep the festivals.
The months of Passover (spring) and Sukkot (autumn). In Tishrei the messengers could not travel on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur, so they got less far.
A rule the Sages added to protect the law. Here, two days of Passover were required so that people would not come to keep Sukkot for only one day.

16.note: Rava used to fast two days for Yom Kippur, in case the month had begun a day later than people in Babylonia thought. Once it turned out he was right. Rav Nahman once fasted the whole of Yom Kippur. In the evening a man came and told him that the next day was Yom Kippur in the Land of Israel. Rav Nahman asked where he was from, and the man said Damihareya. Rav Nahman made a pun on the name, 'Blood will be his end,' and applied to him the verse 'Our pursuers were swifter.' The text does not say what he did the next day.
16.why: These reports follow Levi's discovery that Babylonia kept Yom Kippur a day before the Land of Israel. They show two Sages facing the same doubt about which day was really Yom Kippur.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who regularly fasted two days for Yom Kippur. Once his caution proved right.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage told at the end of his fast that Yom Kippur was actually the next day.

terms.meaning: A name for Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, a full day of fasting.
What the Babylonian Sages called the Land of Israel, which lay to their west.
The man's hometown. Rav Nahman makes a pun on it with the word for blood, because he faces a second day of fasting.

17.note: More than forty pairs of witnesses were on their way to Jerusalem to report seeing the new moon, and someone stopped them in Lod. The mishna says it was Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yehuda says, 'Heaven forbid that Rabbi Akiva stopped them'; it was Zefer, the head of the town of Geder. Rabban Gamliel sent for him, and Zefer was removed from his high office.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage the mishna says stopped the witnesses. Rabbi Yehuda denies it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who says it was not Rabbi Akiva who stopped the witnesses.

people.name: Zefer
people.about: The head of the town of Geder. According to Rabbi Yehuda, he stopped the witnesses and lost his office for it.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The head of the court, who had Zefer removed from office.

terms.meaning: People who saw the first sliver of the new moon and went to the court in Jerusalem to report it, so that the court could declare the new month.
The first written code of Jewish law. The Gemara is a discussion of the mishna, explaining and debating it line by line.

18.note: The Boethusians tried to mislead the Sages about the new moon. They paid two men four hundred dinars to give false testimony: one of their own, and one of the Sages' people. Their man testified and left. The Sages' man was asked to describe the moon, and described it like an animal crouching between rocks, with a calf's head and a deer's horns. He said he had looked, got scared and fallen backward, and that the two hundred dinars he was paid were in his cloak. He said he had done it to warn the Sages. They let him keep the money and ruled that the man who hired him be flogged. From then on they accepted testimony only from witnesses they knew.
18.why: The mishna says that at first the court accepted testimony about the new moon from anyone. The Gemara quotes this baraita to show what went wrong and why that changed.

terms.meaning: A Jewish sect that opposed the Sages and disagreed with them about the calendar.
The court declared a new month only after witnesses came and said they had seen the new moon. False witnesses could therefore shift the dates of the festivals.
Silver coins.
Tied to a post to be flogged.

19.note: Once the sky was covered with clouds, and something that looked like the moon was seen on the twenty-ninth of the month. The people thought it was the New Moon, and the court wanted to declare it. Rabban Gamliel told them that he had a tradition from his grandfather's house: the moon's cycle is never shorter than twenty-nine and a half days plus a little more. That same day the mother of ben Zaza died. Rabban Gamliel gave her a great eulogy, not because she deserved it, but so the people would know the court had not declared the New Moon.
19.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabban Gamliel's family tradition that the moon's path is sometimes long and sometimes short. This baraita shows him using that same tradition to stop the court from declaring the month too early.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The head of the court, who stops the New Moon from being declared too early and uses a eulogy to make the point public.

people.name: Ben Zaza
people.about: A Sage whose mother died that day.

terms.meaning: The first day of a Hebrew month, which the court declared once it accepted that the new moon had been seen. It is a minor festival.
A public speech mourning someone who has died. Eulogies are not allowed on the New Moon, so giving one showed the day was not the New Moon.

20.note: The head of the court had ordered Rabbi Yehoshua to break the day he believed was Yom Kippur. Rabbi Akiva found him distressed and asked why. Rabbi Yehoshua said it would be better to lie sick in bed for twelve months than to have such a decree laid on him. Rabbi Akiva asked to remind him of something Rabbi Yehoshua himself had taught. The Torah says three times that the festivals are what 'you' proclaim, which teaches that the court's date stands even if it errs by accident, on purpose, or because it was misled. Rabbi Yehoshua answered: 'Akiva, you have consoled me, you have consoled me.'
20.why: The mishna says Rabbi Akiva found 'him' distressed, and the Gemara asks which Sage was upset. It cites this baraita to show it was Rabbi Yehoshua, comforted by the rule that the court's date for the month stands.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who finds his teacher distressed and comforts him with his teacher's own teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's teacher, upset at being ordered to break the day he held was Yom Kippur.

terms.meaning: Two Hebrew words that are spelled almost alike. Otam means 'them' and atem means 'you'. Reading 'them' as 'you' teaches that the court has the power to set the dates of the festivals.
The Day of Atonement, a full day of fasting. Its date depends on when the court declared the month had begun.
